title: Mission Families: a cost effective approach to Mission Control System development
organisation: European Space Agency (ESA), European Space Operations Centre (ESOC), Darmstadt; presented at the Ground System Architectures Workshop (GSAW) 2005, 1 - 3 Mar. 2005
status_notes: Slide deck for GSAW 2005 ('Common Solutions' session), 1 - 3 Mar. 2005 (footer on every slide). The date given here is the first day of the workshop.
summary:
An ESOC slide presentation from GSAW 2005 on how ESOC reuses software across mission control systems. The software infrastructure it lists is [SCOS-2000](../scos2000/index.md) for TM processing, TC uplink and verification, archiving and displays, [NCTRS](../scos2000/nctrs-nis.md) as the interface to the ground station network (SLE for non-ESA stations), [GDDS](../scos2000/gdds-and-ddids.md), [TDRS](../scos2000/tdrs.md) and WebRM for web access by external users, and other reusable tools (the XMM file transfer system, the Envisat mission planning system, the CryoSat database editors). Reuse rests on software designed for it, on harmonised spacecraft design and on standards: CCSDS packet TM/TC, the ECSS [Packet Utilisation Standard](../ecss/pus/index.md), [SLE](../ccsds/sle/index.md) and XML.

The core idea is the **'delta' approach**: MCS requirements, design, tests and maintenance are written only as differences from SCOS-2000. The talk then introduces **mission families** (Earth Explorer, Planetary, Observatory), where a family kernel layer on top of SCOS-2000 collects features that similar missions need but that are too specific for SCOS-2000 itself. The worked example is the Earth Explorer family. CryoSat came first as a delta against SCOS-2000, GOCE was built as a delta against CryoSat, which defined the EE kernel, and Aeolus as a delta against that kernel. Requirement counts are given at definition phase (804 in total, 592 kernel and 212 mission-specific) and in the current heritage (680 kernel, 872 in total). The slides list the features each mission contributed, for example an offline database editor and consistency checker, playback TM processing with command verification, on-board queue dump processing, a time correlator, TM data gap identification and automatic schedule execution in NIS/NCTRS. The conclusions stress early involvement of ground teams in spacecraft TM/TC design.

key_points.text: ESOC's reuse rests on infrastructure components designed for reuse, harmonised spacecraft design, and standards: CCSDS packet TM/TC, the ECSS Packet Utilisation Standard, SLE and XML.

The ESOC software infrastructure is listed as SCOS-2000, NCTRS (interface to the ground station network, with SLE for non-ESA stations), GDDS, and TDRS with WebRM for external users such as payload owners.

The ground segment scenario shows NCTRS between ground station and MCS (SCOS-2000) on the Ops LAN, with an FTS and a Generic Data Distribution System behind firewalls on a relay LAN towards external users.

In the 'delta' approach MCS requirements are written only as deltas against the software infrastructure (typically SCOS-2000), and the approach extends to design, development, testing and maintenance.
ESOC mission families: Earth Explorer (low Earth orbit, short visibility), Planetary (long propagation delay, on-board autonomy) and Observatory (long visibility, proposal-based observations).

CryoSat was the first mission to apply the delta approach against SCOS-2000; GOCE was defined as a delta against CryoSat, making the EE Mission Family Kernel concrete; Aeolus was defined against the EE kernel.
At definition phase: CryoSat SRD 406 kernel + 35 specific (441), GOCE SRD 129 + 62 (191), Aeolus SRS 57 + 115 (172); in total 592 kernel and 212 mission-specific requirements (804).
EE requirements heritage: 680 kernel requirements, 35 CryoSat-specific, 42 GOCE-specific and 115 Aeolus-specific, 872 in total.

CryoSat contributions include an offline database editor and consistency check system, a command and parameter identifier extension to the command subsystem, playback TM processing with command verification, and on-board queue dump processing with automatic generation of delete commands.

GOCE contributed TM data gap identification, automatic TM replay and a time correlator; Aeolus contributed weekly consolidation of playback TM and automatic schedule execution in the Network Interface System (NCTRS).
